title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
titleZh: I wish tech companies knew more about me
author: freetonik
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: "Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens... I have never felt anything close to that. I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:

When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern. Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland).

My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services. I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German. The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab.
Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland.
A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.

children.author: hardtke
children.textRawHtml: I would bet that you can train Pandora's algo to respect this preference by thumbing down every vocal techno track.  The music genome annotators will have a boolean for vocals in the analysis.  You'd likely start using recommendation strategies that use the annotations more than normal.  Pandora is still the best for lean back listening.

children.author: ChrisMarshallNY
children.textRawHtml:
Pandora was always the best at figuring out what I wanted to hear; long before AI was a thing, and it's still better.

However, that "non-skip" thing was always a showstopper. Undiscovered music is often obscure for a reason, and I would end up exhausting my skips fairly quickly.

children.author: delecti
children.textRawHtml:
No matter my goal, I found that my Pandora stations always converged on the same endpoint. I always ended up with Ellie Goulding and Dubstep, despite not really liking either of those. It rather killed my interest in the service.

The one exception was an experiment where I gave every single song a thumbs up. It converged on comedy rock (Weird Al, Tenacious D, Flight of the Conchords, etc).

children.author: driverdan
children.textRawHtml:
Way back when I used Pandora I found similar behavior if I gave songs thumbs down. It would converge on a small selection of a few artists and their music. It was really good at some genres if I didn't thumbs up or down many songs.

I've seen the same kind of thing in other services that weight recent choices as a part of their graph based recommendations like Spotify and YouTube. They can get stuck in a feedback loop where the pool of recommendations shrinks to the point where it recommends the same stuff over and over.

children.author: thaumasiotes
children.textRawHtml:
That isn't a feature of Pandora.

I have quite a few channels:

1. Comedy rock, seeded by "Code Monkey". (Mainly Jonathan Coulton and Weird Al Yankovic, but other people sneak in there. The biggest hit, in personal terms, was a song by Matthew Ebel.)

2. Secondary comedy rock, seeded by "Weird Al Yankovic"; this channel is mostly dead. It tried to converge with the main comedy rock channel for obvious reasons.

3. Country (sad), seeded by "She Used To Say That To Me". The main thing on this channel that I personally see as a genre outlier is Mark McGuinn's "Busy Signal", but going to youtube I see that that song is tagged "#countrymusic".

4. Country (happy), seeded by "Emily Harper".

Those two channels also constantly attempt to converge with each other. But they mostly don't try to converge with the comedy rock channel.

5. "Clancy Brothers".

This has blossomed into a more general Irish folk and sea shanty channel.

6. "Steeleye Span".

This one plays Steeleye Span and some other English folk and folk rock music. It constantly tries to play Irish music, though the Clancy Brothers channel does not try to play English folk.

7. "Alan Menken". This one is good at staying separate. It plays showtunes. (And sometimes branches out a little; Annette Funicello's "Pineapple Princess" is on there.)

8. A channel seeded by "Kiss Me", by Sixpence None The Richer. I like the way this song sounds. I was never happy with anything that played on this channel and it's been abandoned.

Within the past several years I have gotten the feeling that Pandora would rather I just have one channel that plays "everything"; there have been attempts at crossing the deeper channel boundaries.

I have never ended up with Ellie Goulding or Dubstep.
